edits.walkthrough_append: **EXAM TRAP:** Set-builder and roster forms must describe the SAME collection — listing {1, 2, 3, 4} for "the set of even numbers between 1 and 4" is wrong, and writing a collection with repeated elements ignores that sets ignore repetition; examiners also ask whether 0 ∈ N or φ ∈ {φ} — membership versus containment distinction carries the mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** A matrix is only an ARRANGEMENT — it has no value until a determinant is taken — so writing "matrix A = 5" confuses the object with its order; also, two matrices are equal only when both order AND every corresponding entry match, which is the standard 1-mark trap.
**EXAM TRAP:** |kA| = kⁿ|A| for an n×n matrix — pulling k out without the power n loses the mark instantly; and |AB| = |A||B| holds only when A and B are square of the same order.
**EXAM TRAP:** A⁻¹ exists only when |A| ≠ 0 — computing an inverse for a singular matrix is impossible, not "very small" — and (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ reverses the order; writing A⁻¹B⁻¹ is the classic slip.

**EXAM TRAP:** X = A⁻¹B, never B⁻¹A — matrix multiplication does not commute, and the system has a UNIQUE solution only when |A| ≠ 0; for |A| = 0 the answer is "no unique solution", not infinity, unless consistency is checked separately.

**EXAM TRAP:** The discriminant test uses b² − 4ac of the GENERAL equation (with the 2h coefficient accounted for): Δ < 0 ellipse, Δ = 0 parabola, Δ > 0 hyperbola — forgetting the 2h convention and computing h² instead of (2h)² flips the answer.

**EXAM TRAP:** A parabola has ONE focus and ONE directrix, eccentricity exactly 1 — and the axis is PERPENDICULAR to the directrix; quoting two foci (that is the hyperbola/ellipse) or e ≠ 1 loses the definition mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** For ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0, the slope pair solves m₁ + m₂ = −2h/b and m₁m₂ = a/b — using h/b instead of 2h/b is the most common slip; and the lines are perpendicular exactly when a + b = 0.

**EXAM TRAP:** A limit is the VALUE APPROACHED, not the value attained — the function need not be defined at the point — and a two-sided limit exists only when left and right limits are EQUAL; quoting f(a) as lim f(x) at a is the standard confusion.

**EXAM TRAP:** P(A|B) multiplies the PRIOR P(B), not P(A) — and P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) only for INDEPENDENT events; using the product rule on dependent diagnostic-test events is exactly the error Bayes' theorem corrects, so writing it backwards loses the derivation mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Commands, questions, wishes, and exclamations are NOT propositions — "Please sit" has no truth value — and an open sentence with an unquantified variable (x + 1 = 2) is not a proposition until the variable is specified; only declaratives with definite truth values qualify.

**EXAM TRAP:** Interest computed on the ORIGINAL principal every period is simple interest — writing compound-interest formulae when the question says "simple", or forgetting to convert the rate and time to the compounding period (rate/4 with quarters), are the two standard financial-mathematics mark-losers.

**EXAM TRAP:** A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt) requires n to match the COMPOUNDING frequency, and effective annual rate = (1 + r/n)ⁿ − 1 — comparing nominal rates without converting to effective rates misorders the answers; also compounding MORE frequently always yields MORE, never less.

**EXAM TRAP:** EMI = P·i·(1+i)ⁿ / ((1+i)ⁿ − 1) uses i as the PER-PERIOD rate (annual rate ÷ 12 for monthly EMIs) — plugging the annual rate directly overstates the EMI; and early EMIs are interest-heavy, so "principal repaid each month is constant" is false.

**EXAM TRAP:** A sinking fund uses the FUTURE-value annuity formula with payments made at the END of each period (ordinary annuity) — using the present-value EMI formula instead, or assuming payments start immediately (annuity due) without adjusting by (1+i), are the two standard slips.

**EXAM TRAP:** A set with n elements has exactly 2ⁿ subsets and 2ⁿ − 1 proper subsets — writing n² subsets, or forgetting that φ and the set itself are both subsets of every set, are the two mistakes counting questions are built to catch.

**EXAM TRAP:** A function sends EVERY domain element to EXACTLY one codomain element — a relation mapping one input to two outputs fails; and one-one (injective) versus onto (surjective) are different tests, so proving only injectivity does not establish a bijection.

**EXAM TRAP:** π radians = 180°, so 1 radian ≈ 57°16′ — multiplying by π/180 when converting degrees TO radians is the standard direction error; and arc length s = rθ only when θ is in RADIANS — using degrees in the arc formula is the classic loss.

**EXAM TRAP:** sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 holds for every θ, but 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ fails where tan is undefined — and sin(2θ) = 2 sinθ cosθ, never 2 sinθ; quoting identity tables without stating the domain of validity loses the rigour mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** The general solution of sinθ = 0 is θ = nπ (n ∈ Z) — solutions must include the PERIOD term; writing only the principal value answers a different question, and forgetting the ± in cosθ = cosα (θ = 2nπ ± α) drops half the solution set.

**EXAM TRAP:** log properties apply only to LOGS of the same base — log(x + y) is NOT log x + log y — and arguments must stay positive: log of a negative number is undefined, so checking the domain after solving is where the last mark lives.

**EXAM TRAP:** arg(z) = tan⁻¹(y/x) needs a quadrant adjustment — the calculator's arctan cannot see which quadrant (x, y) occupies; and arg(0) is undefined, while |z| = 0 for the same point — mixing modulus with argument loses both marks.

**EXAM TRAP:** e^{iθ} = cos θ + i sin θ holds in RADIANS, and de Moivre's theorem (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ applies to INTEGER n directly — for fractional n the result gives only ONE root, not all of them; extending it blindly loses the roots question.

**EXAM TRAP:** The discriminant b² − 4ac decides the number of x-intercepts: D > 0 two roots, D = 0 one (tangent), D < 0 none — and the vertex sits at x = −b/2a, not at −b/a; reading roots off a sketch without checking the sign of a (opening direction) loses the consistency mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** The multiplication principle applies only to INDEPENDENT choices — if one choice removes options for the next, the counts must change at each stage; and "at least one" questions are safest by complement (1 − none), not by direct enumeration.

**EXAM TRAP:** Order matters ⇒ permutation nPr; order does not ⇒ combination nCr — and nCr = nPr/r! must divide out the internal arrangements; using nPr where the question says "select a committee" double-counts every group by r! — the single most common counting slip.

**EXAM TRAP:** Distinct arrangements of a multiset = n!/(p! q! …) — the denominator divides out repetitions of EACH repeated letter; forgetting to include every repeated item's factorial (or adding instead of multiplying the factorials) loses the arrangement mark instantly.

**EXAM TRAP:** The expansion has n + 1 terms with coefficients from row n of Pascal's triangle — the sum of coefficients is 2ⁿ (substitute a = b = 1), NOT n²; and alternating signs appear as (−1)^r, which students routinely drop in (a − b)ⁿ expansions.

**EXAM TRAP:** The general term is T_{r+1} = ⁿC_r a^{n−r} b^r — note that r starts at 0, so the THIRD term has r = 2; equating the POWER of the required variable to n − r, not r, is where most term-finding marks are lost.

**EXAM TRAP:** "Term independent of x" means the power of x is ZERO — set n − 2r = 0 and solve for r, then substitute into ⁿC_r; writing the term with r = 0 (the constant aⁿ) instead shows the power bookkeeping was skipped.

**EXAM TRAP:** In an AP the nth term is a + (n−1)d — the (n−1), not n, is the classic slip; in a GP the common RATIO is found by division and the nth term is ar^{n−1}; summing a GP to infinity is valid only when |r| < 1.

**EXAM TRAP:** Slope m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) — keeping the coordinate order consistent in numerator and denominator is essential; perpendicular lines need m₁m₂ = −1, and PARALLEL lines m₁ = m₂, but a vertical line has UNDEFINED slope, not zero — that is the standard trick option.

**EXAM TRAP:** The distance formula |Ax₀ + By₀ + C|/√(A² + B²) requires the line in GENERAL form — using the coefficients from slope-intercept form without rearranging is the standard error; and the distance is always taken POSITIVE via the modulus.

**EXAM TRAP:** Each intercept form (x/a + y/b = 1) fails when the line passes through the origin — no intercepts exist; choosing the form that fits the given data (two points, slope-point, intercepts) then converting to general form is the exam-efficient sequence.

**EXAM TRAP:** In x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 the centre is (−g, −f) — the MINUS signs are the classic slip — and radius √(g² + f² − c) needs g² + f² ≥ c for a real circle; quoting a negative radius signals an imaginary circle.

**EXAM TRAP:** Substituting a point into the circle's equation decides INSIDE (< r²), ON (= r²), or OUTSIDE (> r²) — using distance-from-centre without squaring, or comparing against r instead of r², flips the classification; three collinear points give NO circle, which is the standard trick option.

**EXAM TRAP:** The circle's diameter form (x − x₁)(x − x₂) + (y − y₁)(y − y₂) = 0 works only when the two points are DIAMETRICALLY OPPOSITE — using it for any two points on the circle draws the wrong locus; the centre-bisects-diameter check verifies the setup.

**EXAM TRAP:** A tangent touches at ONE point and is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact; the condition for y = mx + c to be tangent is c² = r²(1 + m²) — substituting the wrong sign convention or forgetting the point-of-contact perpendicularity loses the tangent mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Three points determine a circle only when they are NON-COLLINEAR — plug each point into x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 and solve the linear system in g, f, c; if the determinant vanishes the points are collinear and NO circle exists — the standard trick case.

**EXAM TRAP:** A parabola's eccentricity is exactly 1 — values 0 < e < 1 give an ellipse and e > 1 a hyperbola — and the latus rectum length is 4a for y² = 4ax, not 2a; conflating the conics' foci counts (1 versus 2) is the standard definition trap.
